c.tagline: A slender coral necklace of a capital, ringing an impossibly blue lagoon.

taxi.fareNote: Shared taxis run the length of the main road for a small flat fare (about $0.75-1); private/negotiated hire costs more, especially at night or out to Laura.

emergency.police: 625-8666 (Majuro Police HQ; there is no nationwide 911-style number)
emergency.medical: 625-3355 / 625-4144 (Majuro Hospital, Ministry of Health & Human Services)
emergency.note: Ambulance coverage is very limited and slow; for urgent injuries a taxi to Majuro Hospital in Delap is often faster.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_desc: Majuro's compact commercial core along Uliga Road, with the main shops, banks, dive/boat operators and the flagship Hotel Robert Reimers clustered together; suits travelers who want walkable convenience.
The lagoon-side government district holding the Capitol (Nitijela), ministries and the atoll's largest resort; suits business travelers and anyone wanting waterfront sunset views close to services.
The denser, more residential eastern end of the Delap-Uliga-Djarrit strip running out to Rita; quieter and more local, suiting budget travelers and longer-stay visitors.
A 45-minute drive west past the airport to the widest white-sand beach on the atoll and a laid-back village feel; suits beach lovers and anyone wanting a rural escape.
Private lagoon islets reachable only by boat, from a simple family-run cottage to an ultra-exclusive private-island retreat; suits honeymooners, divers and travelers chasing total seclusion.

water.note: Tap water is not safe to drink due to bacterial contamination risk; use bottled water.

sys.n: Marshall Islands Shipping Corporation Field-Trip Ships

transit.pay: There is no fare card or app; visitors pay cash in USD directly to the driver. Shared taxis (functioning as the de facto bus system) charge a small flat per-ride fee along the main road, while private hire is negotiated on the spot. Inter-atoll ferry tickets are bought directly from the shipping company office in Delap.
transit.hours: Shared taxis run informally roughly 6am-11pm with no fixed timetable; there is no night service after that aside from pre-arranged private rides.
transit.note: Majuro has no rail or formal bus network - getting around the narrow atoll strip relies on shared taxis, private taxis, walking, or bicycles.

bus: No formal public bus network; shared taxis serve this role along the main road
ferry: Marshall Islands Shipping Corporation inter-atoll field-trip ships

airport.name: Marshall Islands International Airport (Amata Kabua Int'l, MAJ)
rentals: RRE Rent-a-Car (Robert Reimers Enterprises, arranged through Hotel Robert Reimers)

tip.r: Tipping is not customary in the Marshall Islands; it's neither expected nor practiced at most restaurants, hotels, or taxis.

food.name: Grilled Yellowfin Tuna and Sashimi
food.desc: Majuro is the world's busiest tuna transshipment port, so yellowfin comes off the boats hours old, sliced raw for sashimi or grilled with soy and lime.

places.name: Tide Table Restaurant
places.note: Lagoon-side dining room that has been Majuro's standby for decades; tuna is the thing to order.

places.name: Enra Restaurant
places.note: Popular for seafood and for cultural nights with Marshallese dance; fresh tuna features on the menu.

places.name: Marshall Islands Resort
places.note: Waterfront hotel restaurant serving sashimi platters and grilled fish with ocean views.

food.name: Ma and Bwiro (Breadfruit)
food.desc: Breadfruit is the great Marshallese staple: sliced and boiled as ma, or pit-fermented into dense, tangy bwiro that keeps for months at sea.

places.name: Frank K's Restaurant
places.note: One of the best places in town for traditional island plates including cooked breadfruit.

places.name: Laura to Ajeltake road food stands
places.note: The greatest concentration of traditional food and fruit stands on the atoll; breadfruit sold in season.

places.name: Majuro Saturday market
places.note: Vendors come in from outer atolls with breadfruit, taro and pandanus; busiest and best on Saturdays.

food.name: Reef Fish Baked in Coconut Cream
food.desc: Parrotfish, grouper or trevally from the lagoon wrapped in banana leaf with coconut cream and lime, then baked or steamed until it flakes apart.

places.name: Enra Restaurant
places.note: Traditional preparations of local reef fish, often on the cultural-night buffet.

places.name: Tide Table Restaurant
places.note: Local catch cooked island-style alongside a broader menu; convenient central location.

places.name: Ri-Wut Corner
places.note: Neighbourhood local eatery serving everyday Marshallese plates of fish, rice and coconut dishes.

food.name: Banke Kalel (Pumpkin in Coconut Milk)
food.desc: Local pumpkin simmered soft in thick coconut milk until sweet and silky, served as a side with fish and rice. A homely Marshallese favourite.

places.name: Frank K's Restaurant
places.note: Known for island favourites like banke kalel that rarely appear on tourist menus.

places.name: Ri-Wut Corner
places.note: Local plate lunches with rotating coconut-milk vegetable dishes at everyday prices.

places.name: Majuro Saturday market
places.note: Home cooks sell prepared coconut dishes alongside the produce stalls.

food.name: Chukuchuk
food.desc: Balls of sticky cooked rice rolled in freshly grated coconut, eaten as a snack or alongside fish. Simple, sweet and served at nearly every gathering.

places.name: Ri-Wut Corner
places.note: Chukuchuk is a standard item at local takeaway counters like this one.

places.name: Majuro Saturday market
places.note: Stallholders sell chukuchuk by the bag; good with grilled fish from a neighbouring stall.

places.name: Laura to Ajeltake road food stands
places.note: Roadside stands on the drive to Laura beach sell coconut snacks and rice balls.

food.name: Rice, Corned Beef and Johnnycake
food.desc: Majuro's everyday plate. With little arable land, imported rice, tinned meat and flour sit beside local fish; fried johnnycake is the standard breakfast.

places.name: Frank K's Restaurant
places.note: Straightforward local plate lunches that reflect what Majuro actually eats day to day.

places.name: DAR Coffee Corner
places.note: Cafe doing baked goods including johnnycake-style breads, banana bread and savoury scones.

places.name: Roadside johnnycake stands
places.note: Morning stands fry johnnycake to order and serve it with corned beef and coffee.

food.name: Fresh Coconut (Ni)
food.desc: Green drinking coconuts machetted open on the spot. On a coral atoll with no rivers, coconut water has always been the everyday thirst-quencher.

places.name: Laura to Ajeltake road food stands
places.note: Stands along the west end sell drinking nuts cut fresh; the classic stop on the drive to Laura.

places.name: Majuro Saturday market
places.note: Piles of green nuts sold by outer-island vendors; opened for you while you wait.

places.name: Laura Beach
places.note: Picnic spot at the atoll's western tip where vendors sell coconuts to weekend crowds.

food.name: Jekaro (Coconut Sap Toddy)
food.desc: Sweet sap tapped from the coconut flower spathe at dawn, drunk fresh and unfermented or boiled down into thick jekmai syrup. A skilled traditional craft.

places.name: Laura to Ajeltake road food stands
places.note: Rural west end is where tapping still happens; stands sell fresh jekaro and jekmai syrup.

places.name: Majuro Saturday market
places.note: Bottles of jekaro and coconut syrup appear on market mornings when supply allows.

places.name: Enra Restaurant
places.note: Cultural nights sometimes include traditional coconut drinks and demonstrations of tapping.

landmarks: Laura Beach
At the far western tip of Majuro atoll, this stretch of soft white sand and clear lagoon water is widely considered the most beautiful beach on the island, perfect for a relaxed day trip.
Alele Museum and Public Library
This small national museum preserves Marshallese canoe-building traditions, WWII history, and cultural artifacts, offering visitors a quick but rich introduction to the islands' story.
WWII Japanese Bunkers and Relics
Rusting gun emplacements and concrete bunkers scattered around the atoll are haunting reminders of Majuro's role in the Pacific theater of World War II.
Majuro Peace Park
A quiet memorial park honoring those lost in WWII's Pacific campaign, with plaques and monuments set against the lagoon's calm waters.
Marshall Islands Capitol Building
The seat of the Marshallese government is a modern landmark reflecting the young nation's pride, and a good stop for understanding the country's path to independence.
Uliga District Waterfront
The atoll's main commercial hub buzzes with shops, restaurants, and harbor activity, giving a real feel for daily life strung along Majuro's narrow strip of land.
Delap-Uliga-Djarrit (DUD) Causeway Drive
This scenic road strings together Majuro's main urban villages along a slender ribbon of land, with ocean on one side and lagoon on the other for much of the drive.
Rita Point
At the eastern end of the atoll, this breezy point offers dramatic views where open ocean swells crash against the reef just steps from the lagoon's calm.
Majuro Lagoon
The vast, glassy lagoon at the heart of the atoll is ideal for snorkeling, sailing, and watching spectacular sunsets over the water.
Assumption of Mary Catholic Church
A modest but locally beloved church that reflects the deep Christian faith woven into Marshallese community life, with a welcoming congregation open to visitors.

train.note: There are no railways in the Marshall Islands. Arrive by air into Marshall Islands International Airport on Majuro, served by the United Island Hopper route between Honolulu and Guam and by Nauru Airlines. There is no rail anywhere in Micronesia.

bus.note: No international coaches. Majuro's shared taxis run up and down the single road along the atoll for a flat fare, flagged down anywhere - this is effectively the public transport system. There is no terminal and no scheduled bus service.

intl.to: Outer atolls - Arno, Mili, Jaluit & Ebeye (Marshall Islands) - irregular field-trip ships
intl.op: Marshall Islands Shipping Corporation — tickets at the Majuro dock

ferry.note: There is no scheduled international ferry. The government field-trip ships to the outer atolls are the only sea transport and run on no fixed timetable - voyages can take days or weeks and are announced locally, so they suit the flexible rather than the scheduled. Small boats cross Majuro lagoon to Arno on request.

half.name: Eneko Island
half.blurb: A small uninhabited islet a short boat ride from Majuro's lagoon, used for day picnics and snorkeling over shallow reef.

full.name: Arno Atoll
full.blurb: A coral atoll east of Majuro reached by boat across the lagoon, with traditional villages and one of the region's few surfable breaks.
